headline: Tachiba is compared on its page to English standpoint.
Tsugu, “to pour”, is cognate with 継ぐ (tsugu).
Manabu is 真似 (mana, “imitating, copying”) plus ぶ (-bu, “to seem like, to act like”): “to learn” as “to imitate”.
Motomeru is from the Classical Japanese verb 求む (motomu).
Kandenchi is 乾 (kan) plus 電池 (denchi).
Ōjo is Middle Chinese 王女, literally “king + female”, the kan'on reading.
Hori is the continuative stem of 掘る (horu, “to dig”).
Koshikakeru is 腰 (koshi, “hips, lower back”) plus 掛ける (kakeru, “to rest on”).
Sumō is derived from the Old Japanese verb 争ふ (sumapu), “to contend, resist, compete”.
Ume is probably ultimately from Middle Chinese 梅, and was often spelled む (mume) from the Heian period.
Baibai is borrowed from English bye-bye, attested from at least the 1930s.
Hinode is 日 (hi, “sun”) plus の (no) plus 出 (de, “coming out”).
Harau is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 波羅賦.
Kaiketsu is 解 (kai, “to solve”) plus 決 (ketsu, “to decide”).
Tada, “free of charge”, is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Itameru is いた (ita, “painful”, root of 痛い) plus -meru.
Ton is an internationalism; see English ton.
Mairu, the humble “to go”, is a compound of mawi (參, “to go, particularly to the place or person of a social superior”) and 入る (iru).
Kōtō gakkō is 高等 (kōtō, “high level”) plus 学校 (gakkō, “school”).
Meshi is the continuative stem of 召す (mesu, “to call; to eat”).
Kikansha is 機関 (kikan) plus 車 (sha).
Tomeru, “to stop”, is a doublet of 泊める (tomeru).
Karai is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, from Proto-Japonic *kara.
Futa is spelled 蓋上山 for Mount Futagami in the Man'yōshū of circa 759, from Proto-Japonic *pota.
Naderu is from the Old Japanese verb 撫づ (nadu → nazu).
Sayōnara is shortened from 左様ならば (sayō naraba), literally “if that's the way it is”.
Kyū, “ex-”, is from Middle Chinese 舊 (MC gjuwH).
Yoru, “to come from”, is cognate with 寄る (yoru, “to approach”) and 拠る (yoru, “to be based on”).
Han, “size of paper”, is from Middle Chinese 判.
Tsukiataru is 突き (tsuki), the stem of 突く (tsuku, “to poke, push, prod, ram”), plus 当たる (ataru, “to hit”).
Kōfun, “excitement”, began as kaupun.
